adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:148 — Failed result processing is unconditionally marked complete, so transient exceptions allow Kafka offsets to advance and permanently discard the result.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the OrderedQueueWorker.run() method (lines 117-148), the finally block at line 145 unconditionally calls self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset) regardless of whether processing succeeded or failed. When an exception occurs in result_processor (caught at line 140-143), the offset is still marked complete. This means failed messages will have their offsets committed, causing permanent data loss since Kafka will advance past those messages. The test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling test at line 1858 actually expects this behavior (asserts no commits happen), but the implementation does mark offsets complete on error, which would eventually lead to commits.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:185 — Every worker queue is unbounded, so a slow or poisoned grouping key can let the consumer drain Kafka into memory until the process is OOM-killed.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that FixedQueuePool creates queues using `queue.Queue()` without any maxsize parameter (line 185: `work_queue: queue.Queue[WorkItem[T]] = queue.Queue()`). This creates unbounded queues. If a particular group_key consistently hashes to the same queue and that queue's worker is slow or blocked, messages will accumulate in memory without limit. The submit() method at line 199 uses `work_queue.put(work_item)` which will never block on an unbounded queue. This is a real correctness/reliability issue - a slow consumer for one group could cause OOM.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:317 — Any decoder, grouping, or enqueue exception is converted into a completed offset, silently dropping malformed messages and all traffic after a queue-pool failure.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at lines 299-320 in queue_consumer.py, the submit method has a try/except that catches any Exception during decoding, grouping, or queue submission. In the except block (lines 317-320), it marks the offset as both added and completed, effectively dropping the message silently. This means malformed messages or any processing errors will be silently skipped rather than causing a retry or alerting. The finding correctly identifies this as problematic behavior - errors are converted to completed offsets, which could lead to silent data loss.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:233 — Shutdown sets the worker loop guard before draining queued work and stops commits first, so a routine shutdown can abandon the backlog and replay already-finished in-flight work.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the shutdown sequence in the diff: In FixedQueuePool.shutdown() (lines 218-230), it first sets worker.shutdown = True for all workers, then calls q.shutdown(immediate=False) on queues, then joins workers. In SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (lines 333-336), it sets shutdown_event, joins commit_thread, then calls queue_pool.shutdown(). The issue is that setting shutdown_event stops the commit loop before the queue is fully drained. The commit_loop checks shutdown_event.is_set() in its while condition, so once close() sets it, no more commits happen. Meanwhile, workers may still be processing items from the queue. This means: 1) Items still in queues when shutdown starts may not get their offsets committed, 2) The commit thread stops before final offset commits can happen. This could lead to message replay on restart since processed work won't have its offsets committed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py:1916 — The failure test exits only 200 ms after processing although commits run every second, so it silently passes before the implementation commits the failed offset.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the test `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` around line 1870-1916, after processing completes it waits only 0.2 seconds (`time.sleep(0.2)`) before checking commits. However, the commit loop in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop` runs every 1.0 second (`self.shutdown_event.wait(1.0)`). This means the test may pass before the commit loop has a chance to commit the failed offset, making the assertion `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` unreliable - it could pass simply because the commit hasn't happened yet, not because the implementation correctly handles errors.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py:133 — The factory shares one queue pool across assignment-scoped strategies even though closing the first strategy permanently shuts that pool down before the next rebalance-created strategy uses it.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, the queue_pool is created in __init__ at line 133 and stored as an instance variable on the factory. In create_thread_queue_parallel_worker (line 241), it creates a SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy that references self.queue_pool. The shutdown() method at line 182-184 calls queue_pool.shutdown() and sets self.queue_pool = None. However, the factory's create_with_partitions method can be called multiple times during rebalances (it's a ProcessingStrategyFactory pattern). If the first strategy is closed (which calls queue_pool.shutdown via the strategy's close method), the queue_pool workers are shut down. But the factory still exists and could create new strategies on rebalance. Looking at SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() at line 330, it calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(). This means when a strategy is closed during rebalance, it shuts down the shared queue_pool, but the factory might try to create a new strategy using the same (now shutdown) pool. This is a real bug in the lifecycle management.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py:249 — The commit adapter drops Arroyo's `force` parameter, so the strategy cannot force-flush staged offsets during assignment revocation or shutdown.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at line 249 in the diff, the commit_offsets function is defined as `def commit_offsets(offsets: dict[Partition, int]):` and calls `commit(commit_data)` without passing the `force` parameter. The Arroyo Commit type signature typically includes a `force` parameter for flushing staged offsets during revocation/shutdown. The test code at line 1780 shows the expected signature: `def track_commits(offsets: Mapping[Partition, int], force: bool = False) -> None:`. By not accepting and forwarding the `force` parameter, the adapter cannot properly handle forced commits during consumer shutdown or partition revocation, which could lead to offset commit failures in those scenarios.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:335 — close` blocks and stops workers before draining accepted work while `join` ignores its timeout, violating Arroyo's staged graceful-shutdown contract.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, the `close()` method at line 335 sets `shutdown_event`, joins the commit thread, then calls `queue_pool.shutdown()`. The `shutdown()` method of FixedQueuePool sets worker.shutdown=True and calls q.shutdown() which stops workers. However, `join()` at line 345 just calls `self.close()` and ignores the timeout parameter entirely. According to Arroyo's contract, `join(timeout)` should wait for in-flight work to complete within the timeout, but this implementation immediately shuts down workers without draining the queues first. The `close()` method should prepare for shutdown while `join()` should actually wait for completion with the timeout. This is a real defect in the shutdown sequence.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py:136 — The new CLI mode accepts non-positive `--max-workers`, interpreting zero as 20 and negatives as an empty pool that acknowledges every submission without processing it.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at line 136 in the diff: `num_queues=max_workers or 20`. When max_workers is 0, the expression `0 or 20` evaluates to 20 (falsy value triggers the default), so zero is handled. However, for negative values like -1, `-1 or 20` evaluates to -1 (truthy), which would be passed to FixedQueuePool. Looking at FixedQueuePool.__init__, it creates `range(num_queues)` workers - with a negative number, this creates an empty range, meaning no workers/queues are created. The submit() method would still add items to offset_tracker and try to put items in self.queues[queue_index], but with an empty queues list, this would cause an IndexError. The finding's claim about 'acknowledging every submission without processing' is not quite accurate - it would actually crash. But the core issue about non-positive max_workers being problematic is valid.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:149 — Failed result processing is marked complete in `finally`, so the commit loop permanently acknowledges messages whose worker raised.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the OrderedQueueWorker.run() method (lines 119-148), the finally block at line 147 calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)` regardless of whether processing succeeded or failed. When an exception occurs in `self.result_processor(self.identifier, work_item.result)` at line 131, it's caught by the broad `except Exception` at line 138 which only logs the error, then the finally block marks the offset as complete. This means failed messages are acknowledged and will be committed, causing data loss since the failed message won't be reprocessed. The test `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` at line 1858 even verifies this behavior by asserting that after an error, no commits happen - but this is because the test expects both messages to complete (one with error, one without), and the assertion `len(committed_offsets) == 0` actually passes because the commit loop hasn't run yet, not because failed messages aren't marked complete.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py:133 — The single factory-owned pool is shut down by strategy close and then reused on the next partition assignment, causing post-rebalance submissions to be dropped and committed.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, the FixedQueuePool is created once in __init__ (line 133) and stored as factory.queue_pool. The shutdown() method (lines 180-183) calls queue_pool.shutdown() and sets queue_pool = None. However, create_with_partitions can be called multiple times (e.g., after rebalances), and create_thread_queue_parallel_worker (lines 241-254) asserts self.queue_pool is not None. After shutdown is called (which sets queue_pool to None), any subsequent call to create_with_partitions would fail the assertion or cause issues. The strategy's close() method calls queue_pool.shutdown(), and if the factory is reused after a rebalance, the pool would already be shut down. This is a real bug where the pool lifecycle doesn't match the expected usage pattern of the factory being reused across partition assignments.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:317 — Submission failures from grouping or queue insertion are converted to completed offsets, silently dropping those messages.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at lines 303-320 in queue_consumer.py, the submit method has a try/except that catches any Exception during message processing. In the except block (lines 313-320), when an error occurs (which could include failures in grouping_fn or queue_pool.submit), the code marks the offset as both added and completed, effectively treating the message as successfully processed. This means if there's an error during grouping or queue submission, the message is silently dropped and the offset will be committed, causing data loss. The finding accurately identifies this as a problem - submission failures are converted to completed offsets, silently dropping messages.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:233 — Graceful shutdown tells workers to exit before draining queues and stops commits first, so accepted work can be abandoned and completed shutdown work remains uncommitted.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the close() method (lines 329-332), it sets shutdown_event which stops the commit_thread, then joins the commit_thread, then calls queue_pool.shutdown(). In queue_pool.shutdown() (lines 229-241), it sets worker.shutdown=True for all workers, then calls q.shutdown() on queues, then joins workers. The issue is that the commit_thread is stopped BEFORE the queue_pool finishes draining - any work completed after the commit_thread stops will not have its offsets committed. Additionally, setting worker.shutdown=True before draining means workers may exit their loop before processing all queued items. This is a real ordering bug where work can be lost or uncommitted during shutdown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:185 — Every work queue is unbounded, so the strategy never applies Arroyo backpressure and sustained lag can grow until the consumer exhausts memory.

adjudication.rationale: The finding is accurate - looking at line 185 in queue_consumer.py, the FixedQueuePool creates queues with `queue.Queue()` which are unbounded by default. The docstring at line 232 claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' but unbounded queues never fill up. The SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() method at line 280 puts items directly into queues without any blocking or size checks. This means if processing is slower than consumption, memory will grow unbounded. This is a legitimate architectural concern introduced by this diff - the code claims backpressure but doesn't implement it. However, this is a design/architecture issue rather than a correctness bug since the code will function correctly under normal load.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:338 — The strategy shuts down a factory-owned shared pool that the factory also shuts down and reuses across strategy instances, leaving resource ownership ambiguous and rebalance lifecycle unsafe.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real ownership issue. Looking at the diff: 1) The factory creates `self.queue_pool` in `__init__` (line 131-135 in result_consumer.py), 2) The factory's `shutdown()` method calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` and sets it to None (lines 182-184), 3) The `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` method also calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` (line 338 in queue_consumer.py). This creates a double-shutdown scenario where both the strategy and factory can shutdown the same pool. Additionally, during Kafka rebalances, `create_with_partitions` is called multiple times but the factory reuses the same `queue_pool` instance, meaning a new strategy would share the pool with potentially still-running old strategies. This is a legitimate resource ownership bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:344 — join` ignores its timeout and reruns the entire close sequence, violating the staged ProcessingStrategy lifecycle and defeating callers' shutdown budget.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, the `join` method at line 344 simply calls `self.close()` and ignores the `timeout` parameter entirely. The `close()` method itself has hardcoded timeouts (5.0 seconds for commit_thread.join and internal shutdown timeouts). This means callers cannot control the shutdown budget - if they pass a shorter timeout expecting quick termination, it will still wait up to the hardcoded 5+ seconds. Additionally, calling `close()` from `join()` means the full close sequence runs again if close() was already called, which could cause issues. This is a real defect where the timeout parameter is completely ignored.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:31 — The unused `message` field needlessly couples the generic work item to Kafka payload types and retains the original payload for the queue lifetime.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims the `message` field is 'unused', but looking at the diff, the `WorkItem` dataclass is defined with a `message` field at line 31, and this field is populated when creating WorkItem instances (e.g., lines 295-299 in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()). While the field may not be actively used in the current processing logic shown, it's part of a new data structure being introduced. The claim that it 'needlessly couples' or causes memory issues is speculative - the field could be intentionally included for future use, debugging, or extensibility. This is at most a minor design observation, not a verifiable defect or important issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:222 — wait_until_empty` is dead code and its queue-size check cannot account for in-flight worker items, so it should be removed instead of presenting an unsafe lifecycle API.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, `wait_until_empty` is defined at line 222 in queue_consumer.py and checks `self.get_stats()['total_items'] == 0` which only checks queue sizes via `q.qsize()`. The method is indeed not called anywhere in the production code shown in the diff - it's only used in tests. The concern about in-flight worker items is valid: a worker could have taken an item from the queue (reducing qsize) but not yet completed processing it. However, this is more of a design/API concern than a bug since the method isn't used in production code. The finding correctly identifies dead code that has a semantic issue, making it an important non-bug architectural concern.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:185 — Every worker queue is unbounded, so Kafka ingestion can retain unlimited decoded results, original messages, and offset entries when processing falls behind until the consumer OOMs.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that FixedQueuePool creates queues using `queue.Queue()` without any maxsize parameter (line 185: `work_queue: queue.Queue[WorkItem[T]] = queue.Queue()`). This creates unbounded queues. The WorkItem dataclass stores the partition, offset, result, and the original message. If processing falls behind ingestion, these queues will grow without limit, potentially causing OOM. The submit method at line 199 uses `work_queue.put(work_item)` which will never block on an unbounded queue. This is a real defect - there's no backpressure mechanism to prevent memory exhaustion when workers can't keep up with message ingestion.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:83 — Each commit pass rescans the full retained offset set and later copies it, turning a blocked commit frontier into sustained O(n) CPU and allocation work as backlog grows.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that get_committable_offsets() at line 83 iterates through all_offsets with a range loop from min to max offset, and later creates a new set copy in mark_committed(). When there's a blocked commit frontier (e.g., one offset stuck while many more accumulate), this becomes O(n) where n is the number of retained offsets. This is a valid performance/scalability concern for the new code, though not a correctness bug. The code works correctly but could have performance issues under backpressure scenarios.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:149 — A processor exception still completes the offset in `finally`, so failed results are committed without any retry.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in queue_consumer.py lines 130-149, the OrderedQueueWorker.run() method has a try/except/finally block where the finally clause always calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)`. This means even when an exception occurs during `self.result_processor(self.identifier, work_item.result)` (caught by the broad `except Exception` at line 145), the offset is still marked as complete. This allows the offset to be committed even though processing failed, meaning failed messages are lost without retry. The test `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` at line 1858 actually verifies this behavior - it expects that after an exception, offsets are NOT committed, but the current implementation would commit them.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:185 — Each worker queue is unbounded, so sustained downstream slowness can grow the backlog until the consumer exhausts memory.

adjudication.rationale: The finding is accurate - looking at line 185 in queue_consumer.py, the code creates `queue.Queue[WorkItem[T]] = queue.Queue()` without any maxsize parameter, making it unbounded. This is a legitimate architectural concern: if downstream processing is slow, messages will accumulate in these queues without limit, potentially causing memory exhaustion. This is a real concern introduced by this diff, though it's a design/architecture issue rather than a bug since the code functions as written. The finding correctly identifies specific code in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:233 — Shutdown sets every worker's exit flag before winding down its queue, causing workers to abandon queued messages instead of draining them.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the shutdown method in FixedQueuePool (lines 229-240), it first sets worker.shutdown = True for all workers, then calls q.shutdown() on queues, then joins workers. In OrderedQueueWorker.run() (lines 117-143), the worker checks 'while not self.shutdown' and also catches queue.ShutDown. The issue is that setting shutdown=True before draining queues means workers will exit their loop on the next iteration check, potentially before processing all queued items. The queue.shutdown(immediate=False) is called after the shutdown flag is set, so workers may see shutdown=True and exit before the queue signals them to drain. This is a real ordering bug that could cause message loss.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:317 — Any grouping or enqueue failure is swallowed and its offset is marked complete, silently acknowledging work that was never processed.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at lines 303-320 in queue_consumer.py, the submit method has a try/except block where any exception during decoding, grouping, or enqueueing is caught and the offset is immediately marked as both added and completed (lines 315-318). This means if grouping_fn raises an exception or queue_pool.submit fails, the message is silently acknowledged without being processed. The comment says 'Error submitting message to queue' but the code marks the offset complete, effectively losing the message. This is a real bug - work that failed to enqueue is marked as successfully processed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:338 — Closing a strategy permanently shuts down the factory-shared queue pool, so a replacement strategy created after a rebalance cannot process messages.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, in result_consumer.py the queue_pool is created once in __init__ when mode is 'thread-queue-parallel' (lines 128-133). In queue_consumer.py, the close() method at line 335-338 calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(). Looking at FixedQueuePool.shutdown() (lines 227-237), it sets worker.shutdown = True and calls q.shutdown() on all queues, then joins workers. Back in result_consumer.py shutdown() method (lines 180-183), it also sets self.queue_pool = None. The issue is that create_with_partitions() is called on each rebalance to create a new strategy, but the queue_pool is shared at the factory level. When close() is called on the strategy (which happens during rebalance), it shuts down the factory's queue_pool. A new strategy created after rebalance would try to use the same (now shutdown) queue_pool, or if shutdown() was called, queue_pool would be None. This is a real bug where rebalancing would break the consumer.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py:136 — Non-positive `--max-workers` values are not validated, allowing a negative value to create no workers and silently discard every submission.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows at line 136: `num_queues=max_workers or 20`. If max_workers is 0 or negative, the `or 20` fallback only handles 0 (falsy), but negative values would pass through. Looking at FixedQueuePool.__init__, it creates `num_queues` queues in a for loop `for i in range(num_queues)`. If num_queues is negative, range() returns empty, creating 0 queues and 0 workers. The submit() method would then fail with IndexError when trying to access self.queues[queue_index] since the list is empty. However, the finding claims submissions would be 'silently discarded' which isn't quite accurate - it would crash. The core issue about missing validation for non-positive values is valid though.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:149 — The failure test waits only 0.2 seconds before the one-second commit loop, so it misses that failed work is marked complete and later committed

adjudication.rationale: The finding points to a real test design issue. Looking at the test `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` (lines 1823-1870), it expects that when processing fails, offsets should NOT be committed. However, examining the `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` method (lines 119-149), the `finally` block always calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)` regardless of whether processing succeeded or failed. This means failed items are marked complete and will eventually be committed. The test waits only 0.2 seconds after processing completes, but the commit loop runs every 1 second, so the test may pass by timing luck rather than correct behavior. This is a legitimate test/design concern - either the behavior is wrong (failed items shouldn't be marked complete) or the test assertion is wrong.
